title: Is TikTok k!lling Youtube Fitness?
summary: A long rant/analysis arguing that YouTube is copying TikTok (removing dislikes, pushing Shorts, dropping watch time from recommendations), shifting toward kids and entertainment. NH argues this will push out informative long-form fitness content and its audience, producing a 'fast food' fitness culture of memes, clowns and marketing that leaves the next generation small.
claims: YouTube removing dislikes is less about free speech than a cultural shift toward copying Instagram and TikTok: positivity amplified, negativity hidden
YouTube fitness won't disappear; what will die is the current informative community and its audience, replaced by a new breed of creators and viewers
YouTube loses money hosting videos, which is why it pushes ads so aggressively and wants to recapture the profitable kid audience that left for TikTok
Kids are the most profitable audience: no ad blockers, they watch ads fully and binge recommendations
Content aimed at kids follows the 'Fortnite formula': bright colors, loud noises, constant movement
Shorts fragment content so people consume more while feeling they spent little time; a short takes as much feed space as a long video
YouTube fitness started around 2009 as purely informative videos and has been progressively invaded and replaced by entertainment
Shorts are almost never informative; they are entertainment, comedy and sketches
The fastest-growing fitness channels of the past five to six months are almost all meme channels
A friend who teaches math to 7-8 year olds finds heavily screen-exposed kids struggle with calculation and abstraction
You cannot build a good physique or get stronger if you cannot focus
When YouTube fitness started, most videos were 15-20 minutes; now short channels of seven minutes or less dominate
There is no such thing as a video being too long if it's pure information; cutting three minutes cuts three minutes of information

Channels that split one long video into many short ones earn more from ads and the algorithm while giving less or worse information, and recycle the same topics (e.g. 15 'best biceps exercise' videos)
YouTube recently dropped total watch time as a key recommendation factor, favouring click-through rate and percentage watched, which advantages very short videos
Short fitness videos can't cover injury prevention, leverages or styles for a lift like the deadlift, only obvious rehashed tips plus gimmicks
Entertainment-first fitness creators tend to also be the ones selling products, which works best on young audiences
NH spends tens of hours researching a topic before making an hour-long video
The view count of his own videos doesn't concern him
Information is the key to size; a generation fed TikTok fitness misinformation will stay small
Lifters watching rambling 2009 videos may build better physiques than people with all of today's technology, because the flood of content has produced no real information
